doc.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Contemporary jazz, Chet Baker and Jimmy Rowles
summary: Hawkins on rock, Chet Baker with Elvis Costello, Jimmy Rowles, Diana Krall.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Right. What’s your opinion of contemporary jazz these days?

I don’t know. I was — Not bad, but you know, for a second there, but Coleman Hawkins made a very interesting statement one time. Rock & roll. “What do you think of rock & roll?” He says, “There’s nothing wrong with that music it just doesn’t have the right people playing it. It’s just straight eights.” And sure enough he was right. You know this guy Elvis Costello? Well I’m watching a show one night and it’s from Ronnie Scott’s. It’s got Chet Baker with Elvis Costello. I says, “What’s this going to sound like?” So he says what Chet did, you know [inaudible] “I don’t have to know the tunes, you just beat them off. But I don’t want any drummer there. And I don’t want any guitar player over there. I want a bass player, but he’s going to play this, and I want a keyboard but he’s got to play the piano. And I’ll play all your rock & roll stuff with those instruments.” And you wouldn’t have believed how good it sounded. What he could make — he could make music out of like — knocking that lamp over. Chet Baker, an absolute genius, without even knowing it. He played so great I couldn’t believe it. And Elvis Costello sang and it was very believable. And some of the most enjoyable music I ever heard, but he cut out the noise. You’ve got to eliminate all the noise and the noisy drummers and the noisy loud bass and the bass player was good. He could play it. He played all the rhythm, and that’s what I think of the contemporary stuff. But if you get right guy playing it forget it. You can get space guys playing. I heard a thing, I don’t know what it’s called but I was riding in a car with Tony Bell who happens to be over here now. And he was driving Mike Moore to a job in England and he played the radio and they were playing this whole thing by Gary Foster, and Jimmy Rowles and they played “The Peacock” on there. And man it was great. Now if that’s contemporary, I’m all for that. But you know, Jimmy Rowles , he could do that in 1944. That’s what he sounded like then. That’s how good he was. That beautiful tone. He was just an advanced genius. Period. Woody always thought that too you know. They were all going for Bill Evans’ time, he says, “Well I had a guy that did that in 1944 you know.” Telling Alan Broadbent, he says, “Who’s that?” He says, “Jimmy Rowles .” This gal Diana Krall, you know her?

She gets a very nice sound on the piano and very good time. She’s one of the best. But she’s singing now so I don’t know what that’s about. But maybe that’s how they’re pushing her. But I think that’s a contemporary player. She has a couple of good guys
